ECOLOGY
Introduction
8.1.1.1 This section presents the ecological baseline conditions within the Assessment
Area, and the assessment results of the potential ecological impacts resulting from
the construction and operation of the Project. The location plan and description of
the project are presented in Figure 1.1 and Section 2 respectively.
8.1.1.2 According to the EIAO-TM and Appendix G of the EIA Study Brief (ESB-373/2025),
baseline conditions for ecological components of the terrestrial environment were
evaluated based on information from available literature and field surveys
conducted for the purposes of this EIA. Measures required to mitigate any identified
adverse impacts are recommended, where appropriate, and residual impacts, if any,
are assessed.
Environmental Legislation, Standards and Guidelines
8.2.1.1 Reference was made to the following HKSAR Government ordinances, regulations,
standards, guidelines and documents when identifying ecological importance of
habitats and species, and evaluating and assessing potential impacts of the Project
on the ecological resources:
• Country Parks Ordinance (Cap. 208) and its subsidiary legislation;
• Forests and Countryside Ordinance (Cap. 96) and its subsidiary legislation, the
Forestry Regulations (Cap. 96A);
• Wild Animals Protection Ordinance (Cap. 170);
• Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance (Cap. 586)
and its subsidiary legislation;
• Chapter 10 of the Hong Kong Planning Standards and Guidelines;
• Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (Cap. 499) and relevant
Annexes 8 and 16 of the associated Technical Memorandum (EIAO-TM);
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 6/2010 – Some Observations on Ecological
Assessment from the Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance
Perspective;
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 7/2023 – Ecological Baseline Survey for Ecological
Assessment;
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 10/2023 – Methodologies for Terrestrial and
Freshwater Ecological Baseline Surveys;
• Drainage Services Department Practice Note No. 3/2021 – Guidelines on
Design for Revitalisation of River Channel;
• Environment, Transport and Works Bureau Technical Circular (Works) (ETWB
TC(W)) No. 5/2005 – Protection of Natural Streams/Rivers from Adverse
Impacts Arising from Construction Works;
• New Nature Conservation Policy;
• Hong Kong Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (2035);

and national legislation:

• The List of Wild Plants and Wild Animals Under Special State Protection under
the Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Protection of Wildlife; and
• The Convention on Biological Diversity (the CBD), and an associated city-level
Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (BSAP) developed by Agriculture,
Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) under the CBD.
• List of Wild Animals under State Protection; and
• List of Wild Plants under State Protection.
Assessment Methodology
Assessment Area
8.3.1.1 The Assessment Area for the purpose of the terrestrial and aquatic ecological
impact assessment included areas within 500 metres from the boundary of the
Project and its associated works (Figure 8.1).
Ecological Survey Methodology
8.3.2.1 A 12-month ecological field survey covering both wet and dry seasons were
conducted to gather updated information on the Assessment Area, and to fill any
information gaps identified within the 500 m Assessment Area. The field surveys
covered flora, fauna and any other habitats/species of conservation importance.
The fauna species were surveyed during the optimal time of the day as stated in
Appendix B of the EIAO-TM Annex 16. All field surveys were carried out in ways
that do not cause any unnecessary stress or damage to the existing habitats and
wildlife.
8.3.2.2 The walk-transects for ecological surveys, freshwater sampling points and locations
for camera traps are indicated in Figure 8.2. The vantage points for flight line
survey are indicated in Figure 8.3. Where coverage by walk-transect was not
possible (e.g. inaccessible areas within private areas, barrack areas where access
is not allowed, hillside areas with limited accessibility and safety concern), high-
power binoculars were used to determine the habitat structure, general vegetation
composition, at a location as close as possible.
Habitat Mapping and Vegetation Survey
8.3.2.3 Terrestrial and aquatic habitats within the Assessment Area were identified, sized
and mapped. Ecological characteristics of each habitat type, including size,
vegetation type, species present, dominant species found, species diversity and
abundance, community structure, ecological value and inter-dependence of the
habitats and species, and presence of any features of ecological importance were
defined and characterised. Representative photographs of the habitat types and/or
any important ecological features identified were taken. A habitat map of suitable
scale (1:1,000 to 1:5,000) showing types and locations of terrestrial and aquatic
habitats within the Assessment Area was prepared from digital aerial photographs.
The habitat map was checked during ground truthing. For areas that are
inaccessible, aerial drones were used to capture photographs and videos to survey
ecological features and verify habitats.

8.3.2.4 Vegetation surveys were conducted by direct observation to record the diversity
and dominance of plant species present in different habitat types. The locations of
any plant species of conservation importance were recorded.
8.3.2.5 Identification of flora species and status in Hong Kong made reference to Xing et
al. (2000), Hu et al. (2003), Lai et al. (2008), Hong Kong Herbarium (2012), and
Hong Kong Herbarium and South China Botanical Gardens (2007; 2008; 2009;
2011).
Avifauna Survey
8.3.2.6 The presence and abundance of all avifauna species in various habitats were
recorded visually and aurally. Avifauna was surveyed quantitatively using the
transect count method along the walk-transect during morning, dusk and night times.
The location of any avifauna species of conservation importance encountered were
recorded, along with notable behaviours (e.g. breeding behaviour such as nesting
and the presence of recently fledged juveniles, roosting, and feeding activities).
8.3.2.7 Ornithological nomenclature follows Carey et al. (2001), Viney et al. (2005), and the
most recent list published by the Hong Kong Bird Watching Society.
Roosting Ardeids and Flight Line Survey
8.3.2.8 Flight line surveys were conducted for Sha Po Night Roost and Ko Po Road Night
Roost at the vantage points, VP1 and VP2, during the peak activity period of ardeids
at night roosts (Figure 8.3). The vantage points are indicative in nature and are
subject to change due to site condition and accessibility upon the exercise of
professional judgement during the course of survey. The flight lines of ardeid
individuals were followed by means of high-power binoculars to identify their landing
locations, whenever possible. In case the ardeids fly out of sight prior to landing,
the locations where they were last seen were recorded. Flight line survey for night
roosts was commenced approximately one hour before sunset and continue until
nightfall. The flight lines, flight height of the flight lines, the return times of the pre-
roosting and night-roosting ardeids, and substrate used at the ardeid night roosts
were recorded. The time of sunset on the date of survey made reference to the
Hong Kong Observatory.
8.3.2.9 Given the potential presence of roosts for ardeids and other avifauna (e.g. Great
Cormorants) within the Assessment Area, the field surveys also focused on
confirming the presence of any potential roosting sites, in particular trees adjacent
to ponds and wetland habitats. No new roosting sites were identified during the
course of the ecological surveys.
Terrestrial Mammal Survey
8.3.2.10 The surveys focused on areas that may potentially be utilised by terrestrial
mammals. Field signs including droppings, footprints, diggings or burrows left by
larger mammals were searched for. Mammal identification was made as accurately
as possible from the field signs encountered. Any mammals directly observed were
recorded. Camera traps were deployed at selected locations as indicated in Figure
8.2.

at potential roosting, commuting, foraging and drinking sites. Bat species was

Herpetofauna (Amphibian and Reptile) Survey
8.3.2.16 Herpetofauna was surveyed along survey transects. Potential microhabitats (e.g.
leaf litter, underneath of rotten logs) were searched. All reptiles and amphibians
sighted were recorded.
8.3.2.17 Amphibian survey was conducted whenever possible on evenings and night time,
focusing on areas suitable for amphibians (e.g. forests, shrublands, grasslands,
streams, catchwaters, ponds and marshes). Acoustic records of amphibians
constitute the majority of data collected, supplemented by visual observation of
eggs, tadpoles and frogs / toads whenever possible.
8.3.2.18 During reptile surveys, careful searches were conducted at the preferrable
microhabitats and refugia of reptiles (e.g. stones, pond bunds, crevices, leaf
litter/debris, rotten log). All reptiles encountered were recorded. In addition to
active searching, observation of exposed, basking and foraging reptiles were made.
8.3.2.19 Nomenclature of amphibian and reptile follows Chan et al. (2005) and Chan et al.
(2006), respectively.
Freshwater Invertebrates and Fish Survey
8.3.2.20 Freshwater invertebrates and fish survey was conducted through active searching

night-time for nocturnal species.

Description of the Environment
Recognised Sites of Conservation Importance
Deep Bay Wetland outside Ramsar Site Priority Site for Enhanced Conservation
8.4.1.1 Deep Bay Wetland outside Ramsar Site is a Priority Site of Enhanced Conservation
under the New Nature Conservation Policy, comprising mainly fishponds. The
Deep Bay Wetland outside Ramsar Site supports species of conservation
importance such as Black-faced spoonbill (Platalea minor). A corner of this Priority
Site of Enhanced Conservation is overlapping with the Project Boundary to the west
of Sha Po.
Lam Tsuen Country Park (LTCP)
8.4.1.2 LTCP was designated in 1979 and spans across Tai Po, Fanling and Yuen Long.
The LTCP occupies 1,520 ha of land in the Northern New Territories (AFCD,
2023a). Plantation stands of exotic tree species such as Taiwan Acacia (Acacia
confusa) and Brisbane Box (Lophostemon confertus), as well as native Machilus
species were established throughout the territory of LTCP. Faunal species of
importance such as Chinese Porcupine (Hystrix brachyura), Chinese Ferret Badger
(Melogale moschata) and Chinese Pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) could be found
within the LTCP. The LTCP is located adjacent to the Project Boundary to the south
of NTM area.

which form an integral part of the wetland ecosystem in the Deep Bay Area.
Wetland Conservation Area
8.4.1.5 Wetland Conservation Area (WCA) comprises existing and contiguous, active or
abandoned fishponds in the Deep Bay Area, along the landward side of the Mai Po
Inner Deep Bay Ramsar Site. The planning intention is to conserve the ecological
value of the fishponds which form an integral part of the wetland ecosystem in the
Deep Bay Area. The WCA lies directly adjacent to the Project Boundary to the west
of Sha Po.
Wetland Buffer Area
8.4.1.6 Wetland Buffer Area (WBA) is located along the landward periphery of the WCA. It
is a designated buffer area of about 500 m along the landward boundary of the
WCA. It is intended to protect the ecological integrity of the fishponds and wetland
within the WCA, and to prevent development that would have a negative offsite
disturbance impact on the ecological value of fishponds. Part of the WBA is situated
within the Project Boundary along the San Tin Highway.
Other Ecologically Sensitive Resources
Inner Deep Bay and Shenzhen River Catchment Important Bird Area (IBA)
8.4.2.1 Mai Po Inner Deep Bay area and the vicinity around Shenzhen River Catchment
was recognised as an Important Bird Area (IBA) by BirdLife International, for its
international significance in terms of the size and trend of bird population. The
recognition was done as an effort to secure long-term conservation of areas that
are important for birds and biodiversity. A mosaic of wetland habitats (total 3,150
ha) was recognised for its global importance, and support to large number of
passage and wintering waterbirds, including species of conservation importance
and threatened species.
Roosting Sites
8.4.2.2 Two night roosts are located within the Assessment Area, namely Sha Po Night
Roost and Ko Po Road Night Roost.
8.4.2.3 For Sha Po Night Roost, ardeids such as Great Egret (Ardea alba), Grey Heron
(Ardea cinerea), Chinese Pond Heron (Ardeola bacchus) and Little Egret (Egretta
garzetta) were observed utilizing trees located at the eastern bank of Kam Tin River
(MTRCL, 2024). Roosting substratum included White Popinac (Leucaena

8.4.2.4 For Ko Po Road Night Roost, ardeids such as Eastern Cattle Egret (Bubulcus
coromandus), Chinese Pond Heron (Ardeola bacchus) and Little Egret (Egretta
garzetta) were observed utilising trees along the southern bank of Kam Tin River

Kam Tin Main Drainage Channel (KTMDC)
8.4.2.5 KTMDC is a channelized section of Kam Tin River. The KTMDC is tidal-influenced
and utilized by various wetland associated bird species such as egrets, sandpipers,
kingfishers and plovers. Winter visitor and migrant, such as Grey-headed Lapwing
(Vanellus cinereus), was often found utilising the channel (MTRCL, 2023). Part of
the KTMDC is located within the Project Boundary.
Sha Po Marsh
8.4.2.6 The Sha Po Marsh is currently managed by a private estate developer, Sun Hung
Kai Properties Limited, as an Ecological Enhancement Area. It is a restored
brackish marsh, where 180 wildlife species were recorded (SHKPL, 2017). The
marsh was reported to support a Near Threatened damselfly species Four-spot
Midget (Mortonagrion hirosei). The Sha Po Marsh is located directly adjacent to
the Project Boundary.
Yuen Long Bypass Floodway Engineered Wetland
8.4.2.7 Yuen Long Bypass Floodway Engineered Wetland (YLBFEW) is located near the
downstream of Yuen Long Bypass Floodway and managed by AFCD since 2006
(DSD, 2019). This wetland was constructed as part of the ecological mitigation
measures for Yuen Long Bypass Floodway Project. The engineered wetland
consists of three main water ponds, a seasonal shallow pond and a permanent
shallow pond. There are also crushed brick and oyster shell ponds, reed beds and
a deep-water pond within the wetland. The dry weather flow of the Bypass
Floodway, after purified by passing through the oyster shells, crushed bricks and
reed bed, flows into the engineered wetland to offer an ecologically enriched habitat
for the wild birds, amphibians and dragonflies (DSD, 2019). The YLBFEW is
situated in approximately 25 m away from the Project Boundary.
West Rail Compensatory Wetland

Area of the Project and is located in approximately 325 m to the east of the Project
Boundary in Kam Tin. This compensatory wetland was created since 2022 to
mitigate for the loss of wetlands in Kam Tin Valley due to the construction of West
Rail in accordance with Environmental Permit No. FEP-24/004/1998/J. The West
Rail Compensatory Wetland is currently maintained and managed by MTR
Corporation.

8.4.2.10 Under the approved EIA for the Northern Link (Register No.: AEIAR-259/2024), a

future Ecological Enhancement Area (EEA) of the Park Yoho Phases 2 and 3

to compensate for the loss of marsh/reed habitat due to the project. The planned

Planned Compensation Wetland for Ngau Tam Mei (NTM) Development Area
8.4.2.11 Under the approved EIA for the NTM Development Area (Register No.: AEIAR-
271/2025, CEDD, 2025), a wetland compensation site of about 3.5 ha has been
identified adjacent to Kam Tin River, between Tsing Long Highway and San Tam
Road at Sha Po area. This site was proposed to accommodate the wetland
compensation requirement of about 2.55 ha under Ngau Tam Mei development,
and is currently a developed area/wasteland habitat overgrown with herbs/shrubs

ecological value. Despite part of the wetland compensation site is overlapping with
the proposed NMH alignment, based on latest project coordination during the
preparation of this EIA Report, “no work zone” is incorporated into the Project
design to delineate areas where no construction activities will be undertaken, direct

8.4.2.12 As recommended in the Study Report of the Strategic Feasibility Study on the

October 2024, the proposed Nam Sang Wai Wetland Conservation Park (WCP) is
part of the proposed WCPs System which serve to conserve the ecological value

modernised aquaculture industry to create more job opportunities for the agriculture
and fisheries industries; promote scientific research on aquaculture to facilitate the
upgrade and transformation of the agriculture and fisheries industries; and provide
ecological education and recreational facilities for the public (AFCD, 2024). The
proposed Nam Sang Wai WCP lies directly adjacent to the Project Boundary.

Literature Review

information, such as Hong Kong Environmental Database (HKED) (EPD, 2025), on
the ecological characteristics of the Assessment Area were collected and reviewed
(Table 8.2). The information collected was evaluated to identify any gaps related

Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)

Habitat and Vegetation
8.5.2.1 A total of 15 habitat types were previously identified within the proposed 500 m
Assessment Area, which included woodland, mixed woodland, shrubland,
grassland, plantation, village/orchard, developed area/wasteland, agricultural land,
seasonally wet grassland, marsh/reed, pond, natural watercourse, semi-natural
watercourse, modified watercourse, mitigation wetland (CEDD, 2025; CEDD &
PlanD, 2024; MTRCL, 2023; MTRCL, 2024; WSD, 2024).
General Description of Habitats within Assessment Area
8.5.2.2 The Project Boundary for Northern Metropolis – San Tin section starts from Kam
Tin River in the southwest, spanning towards the northeast across Ngau Tam Mei,
Ki Lun Tsuen, and ending at Tit Hang near Chau Tau Village. The 500 m
Assessment Area from the Project Boundary mainly covers urbanised habitats
(village and developed area), wooded habitats (across hills and hillside area), with
only a small portion of wetland habitats mainly on the southwest near Kam Tin River
and scattered over the Assessment Area.
8.5.2.3 8.5.2.4 8.5.2.5 Pond habitat was present within the Assessment Area mainly near Nam Sang Wai
and Pok Wai to the west of San Tin Highway, at Ngau Tam Mei (NTM) area, as well
as some scattered ponds near Ki Lun Tsuen. Other wetland habitats previously
recorded include marsh/reed, natural watercourse, semi-natural watercourse and
modified watercourse. These wetland habitats were relatively scattered. While
these habitats supported relatively low diversity and abundance of flora and fauna,
ecological and hydrological linkage between these habitats and ponds were
observed.
Woodland habitats (e.g. woodland and mixed woodland) were mainly found at the
southern part at lower hillside of Kai Kung Leng and Ngau Tam Shan. This habitat
comprised of common tree and herb species. Grassland and shrubland habitats
were mainly found at the northern part at Hadden Hill and Ngau Tam Shan. These
habitats mainly comprise common herb and shrub species.
Urbanised habitats (e.g. developed area/wasteland and village/orchard) were
scattered throughout the Assessment Area. These urbanised habitats consisted of
villages (such as Ngau Tam Mei Tsuen and Ki Lun Tsuen), roads, open storage
areas and garages. These habitats were often subjected to high level of human
disturbance and dominated by exotic and ornamental vegetation.
Fauna
Avifauna
8.5.3.1 The avifauna community in the vicinity of the Assessment Area mainly comprise of
waterbirds and wetland-dependent species recorded near wetland habitats of the
Assessment Area (e.g. pond and watercourse). A total of 62 species of
conservation importance were recorded in previous studies (CEDD & PlanD, 2024;
CEDD, 2025; CEDD and PlanD, 2022; DSD, 2018; MTR, 2024a; MTR, 2024b; WSD,
2024).
Mammal
8.5.3.2 Mammal species previously recorded within the Assessment Area include bats and
non-flying terrestrial mammal species, a total of 20 species of conservation

8.5.3.6 Freshwater species previously recorded within the Assessment Area in aquatic

Overview of Ecological Baseline Conditions
8.6.1.1 Consistent with the findings from literature review, a total of 15 habitat types were
identified during the ecological survey within the 500 m Assessment Area, which
included woodland, mixed woodland, shrubland, grassland, plantation,
village/orchard, developed area/wasteland, agricultural land, seasonally wet
grassland, marsh/reed, pond, natural watercourse, semi-natural watercourse,
modified watercourse, mitigation wetland. Ecological resources within the
Assessment Area are presented in the following sections. A summary of all habitats
identified within the Assessment Area is presented in Table 8.3.

and Fan-leaved Maidenhair (Adiantum flabellulatum) were commonly encountered.

Mixed Woodland
8.6.2.5 Patches of mixed woodland were identified at Tit Hang, Ngau Tam Mei and at the
west of Tsing Long Highway. Mixed woodland habitat was characterized by the tree
canopies which consisted of both exotic and native trees and semi-closed canopies.
Mixed woodland habitat was connected to adjacent developed area/wasteland and
subject to human disturbance.
8.6.2.6 Semi-open canopies ranged from 5 m to 8 m semi-open canopy were recorded and
composed by native tree species such as Chinese Hackberry (Celtis sinensis) and
Camphor Tree (Cinnamomum camphora), scattered with cultivated fruit tree
species such as Jackfruit. Planted exotic tree species such as Paper-bark Tree,
Slash Pine, Brisbane Box and Big-leaved Acacia (Acacia mangium) were also
encountered. Native herb and shrub species such as Chinese Fevervine (Paederia
scandens), Snail Seed (Cocculus orbiculatus), Desmos (Desmos chinensis) and
Wild Coffee, and cultivated shrub species such as Orange-jessamine (Murraya
paniculata) and exotic species such as Lantana were found at the understory.
8.6.2.7 Three flora species of conservation importance, namely Aralia chinensis, Incense
Tree and Lamb of Tartary (Cibotium barometz) were found within this habitat in
Ngau Tam Mei area (Figure 8.5.6 and 8.5.9 refers).
Shrubland
8.6.2.8 Patches of shrubland including mature and tall shrub areas were identified at Tit
Hang, Hadden Hill, Ngau Tam Shan, Kai Kung Leng, and along Tsing Long
Highway. This habitat was often interspersed with contiguous area of grassland.
Part of the hillside shrubland in Hadden Hill, Ngau Tam Mei and Kai Kung Leng was
located within CA. Small extent of the hillside shrubland of Kai Kung Leng was also
located within the LTCP. Native shrub and herb species such as Rose Myrtle
(Rhodomyrtus tomentosa), Wax Tree (Rhus succedanea) and Hong Kong
Hawthorn (Rhaphiolepis indica) were commonly encountered in this habitat.
8.6.2.9 Roadside shrubland at Nam Sang Wai area was succeeded from former pond bund
which has now been overgrown. Weedy species such as White Popinac, Gairo
Morning Glory and Mile-a-minute Weed were commonly encountered. Native tree
and herb species such as White Mulberry (Morus alba), Opposite-leaved Fig and
Many-flowered Silvergrass (Miscanthus floridulus) were also encountered.
8.6.2.10 One flora species of conservation importance namely Incense Tree was recorded
in this habitat to the northeast of Hadden Hill (Figure 8.5.11 refers).
Grassland
8.6.2.11 Grassland habitat identified includes hillside grassland and low-lying grassland.
Extensive hillside grassland was found in Tit Hang, Hadden Hill, Ngau Tam Shan,
Kai Kung Leng, and Ho Hok Shan. In contrast, low-lying grassland was identified at
lowland locations scattered by developed area/wasteland, village/orchard, in Ki Lun
Tsuen, Ngau Tam Mei, and along San Tin Highway. Part of the hillside grassland
in Hadden Hill, Ngau Tam Shan and Ho Hok Shan were located within CA, while
part of the hillside grassland in Kai Kung Leng was located within both CA and
LTCP.
8.6.2.12 The hillside grasslands are susceptible to periodic hill fires, which arrest ecological
succession. Flora composition of these grassland habitats composed of pioneer

Plantation

Agricultural Land
8.6.2.22 Patches of dry agricultural land were identified at Tit Hang, Ki Lun Tsuen, Hang Tau,
Ngau Tam Mei, and along San Tin Highway. Small patches of dry agricultural land
were scattered in Tit Hang and Ki Lun Tsuen while patches of considerable size
were found in Hang Tau and Ngau Tam Mei, with most of them fenced off or
surrounded by village houses. Small scale farming with fruit and crop species was
observed, such as Common Banana, Purple Granadilla (Passiflora edulis) and
Sugar-apple (Annona squamosa). Inactive fields were interspersed among the
active fields. They may be temporarily or permanently abandoned and overgrown
with ruderal herbs such as Green Amaranth (Amaranthus viridis), Guinea Grass
and Redtop.
8.6.2.23 No flora species of conservation importance was recorded within this habitat.
Seasonally Wet Grassland
8.6.2.24 Seasonally wet grassland was identified at the east of Sha Po Marsh. This habitat
was succeeded from poorly drained abandoned agricultural land. This habitat was
wet most of the time in wet season and dry in dry season, while aquatic plant such
as Job's tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), Blunt Signal-grass and Giant Alocasia were
commonly encountered. Exotic weedy species such as White Popinac, Mile-a-
minute Weed and Wedelia trilobata were also encountered.
8.6.2.25 No flora species of conservation importance was recorded within this habitat.
Marsh/Reed
8.6.2.26 Several scattered small areas of marsh/reed habitat were identified, mostly on the
southwest of the Assessment Area, along Kam Tin River to the west of San Tin
Highway. This includes areas within WBA, WCA (such as Nam Sang Wai and Pok
Wai), as well as areas outside WBA and WCA such as Sha Po and Ngau Tam Mei.
8.6.2.27 Most of the marsh/reed habitat within the Assessment Area were naturally derived
from abandoned ponds. The floral diversity was generally low and dominated by
aquatic herbs such as Sessile Alternanthera (Alternanthera sessilis) and Interrupted
Tri-vein Fern (Cyclosorus interruptus), and some ruderal herbs on the edges such
as Napier Grass (Pennisetum purpureum) and Bidens alba. Reed species such as
Common Reedgrass (Phragmites australis) and Burma-reed (Neyraudia
reynaudiana) were occasionally encountered.
8.6.2.28 Sha Po Marsh is a restored brackish marsh, native mangrove species such as
Leather Fern (Acrostichum aureum) and exotic mangrove species such as
Sonneratia spp. were commonly encountered. Native herb species such as Short-
leaved Malacea Galingale (Cyperus malaccensis var. brevifolius) was also
commonly encountered in this restored habitat.
8.6.2.29 No flora species of conservation was recorded within this habitat.

Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)

Pond
8.6.2.30 Similar to marsh/reed, pond habitat was mainly concentrated along Kam Tin River,
to the west of San Tin Highway, and in Ngau Tam Mei. Scattered ponds were
identified in Tit Hang and Ki Lun Tsuen.
8.6.2.31 Majority of the ponds identified to the west of San Tin Highway were located within
WBA, WCA. These ponds are mostly inactive, with a few active fishponds observed
near Pok Wai. For ponds in Ngau Tam Mei, they were located between village
areas, thus relatively fragmented and subject to regular disturbance from adjacent
human activities, except for a few larger ponds west of NTMWTW. Most of the
ponds in Ngau Tam Mei are active fishponds practicing Koi culturing. Limited
vegetation were observed from ponds in both areas (west of San Tin Highway, and
in Ngau Tam Mei), mainly comprising Weedy species such as Blunt Signal-grass
(Brachiaria mutica), Mile-a-minute Weed (Mikania micrantha), while pond bunds in
Ngau Tam Mei also include cultivated fruit tree species such as Longan
(Dimocarpus logan) and Common Banana (Musa x paradisiaca), as well as the
presence of some White Popinac.
8.6.2.32 For Tit Hang and Ki Lun Tsuen, these ponds were relatively small and fragmented,
located adjacent to village and/or urbanised areas. These small ponds supported
limited vegetation, mainly comprising weedy species on the pond bund such as
Guinea Grass (Panicum maximum), White Popinac and Mile-a-minute Weed.
8.6.2.33 No flora species of conservation was recorded within this habitat.
Natural Watercourse
San Tin
8.6.2.34 ST-S3a was an abandoned meander connecting to the eastern bank of Sheung
Yue River and ran through plantation habitat. ST-3a was approximately 5 m to 15

Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)
Northern Metropolis Highway
– Investigation
Environmental Impact Assessment Report – San Tin Section
Identification of Potential Ecological Impacts
Construction Phase – Direct Impact
Direct Loss of Habitat and Vegetation
8.8.1.1 Direct impacts on terrestrial and aquatic habitats would arise from the proposed
alignment, including at-grade works (e.g. roads, slope works, tunnel portals,
ancillary facilities, etc.), viaduct supports (e.g. pile and pier-related works), and
associated temporary works (e.g. works area, temporary access, and storage areas)
with the Project boundary.
8.8.1.2 Around two-thirds of the areas that are subject to direct habitat loss would result
from temporary works such as works areas, temporary access (e.g. haul roads),
and storage area. These temporary works areas would be released and reinstated
upon completion of the construction works as far as practicable. Only a relatively
small areas of habitats would be lost due to the proposed alignment (i.e. at-grade
works and viaduct supports). The extent of direct habitat loss associated with the
proposed alignment and temporary works within the Project Boundary is presented
in Table 8.14 below.
8.8.1.3 Due consideration was given to the land requirements for both temporary at-grade
construction activities and permanent at-grade structures during the development
of the layout design for the Project. Sensitive ecological resources were identified
early in the ecological baseline study, leading to corresponding adjustments to the
alignment and layout of associated works. These adjustments included opting for
tunnel and/or viaduct sections to minimise at-grade works and fine-tuning the
alignment to minimise encroachment on sensitive areas. This approach aimed to
avoid direct impacts on the concerned ecological resources or keep them to a
minimum where possible.
8.8.1.4 A substantial portion of the direct loss area would consist of man-made habitats of
low ecological value, such as developed area/wasteland, grassland, and
village/orchard habitats. In contrast, wetland habitats including marsh/reed, pond,
semi-natural watercourse, and modified watercourse would account for only a small
proportion of the total direct loss area during the construction phase of the Project.

8.8.1.23 Fragmentation refers to the discontinuity of habitat, reducing the carrying capacity
and hindering the movement of wildlife species, resulting in less favourable habitat
for flora and fauna species. Fragmentation of habitat may also result in isolation of
some population of species in the area.
Fragmentation and Isolation of Vegetated Areas
8.8.1.24 Under the Project, the at-grade works at Kai Kung Leng, Ngau Tam Shan and
Hadden Hill may potentially lead to fragmentation of existing vegetated habitats by
obstructing the movement of associated wildlife, such as non-flying mammals and

the proposed works are largely situated along the margins of the wooded habitats.

effectively minimising and avoiding direct impact and fragmentation to the wooded
habitats. As such, the potential fragmentation and isolation impacts arising from

Impact
8.8.2.24 Site formation and construction activities may cause potential water quality impacts
to adjacent watercourses and pond habitats. These include deterioration of water

accidental spills of oil, fuel, or other harmful chemicals. Additionally, construction
works may alter water flow in watercourses outside the Project Boundary.

Impacts on Bird Collision

8.8.4.1 During the operation phase, disturbances such as noise, light and glare, dust, traffic,
and other human disturbances may arise due to the Project. Four recognized sites
of conservation importance (i.e. Deep Bay Wetland outside Ramsar Site Priority
Site for Enhanced Conservation, CA, WCA, and WBA) and four other ecologically
sensitive resources (i.e. proposed Nam Sang Wai Wetland Conservation Park, the
planned wetland compensation site under the Ngau Tam Mei Development, the
planned bat shelter in Pok Wai, and Sha Po Night Roost) are situated within the
Project Boundary. Additionally, other ecologically sensitive resources (i.e.
YLBFEW, Sha Po Marsh, Ko Po Road Night Roost, Important Bird Area, West Rail
Compensatory Wetland, and planned wetland compensation site in Kam Tin for the
Northern Link) are located directly adjacent or outside the Project Boundary. Given
that the proposed alignment would be located along the existing highways in Kam
Tin area, the Project is not expected to result in disturbance levels significantly
different from current conditions. The recognised sites of conservation importance
and ecologically sensitive resources mentioned above are already subject to
substantial and ongoing human activities, including existing roads, high traffic
volumes, nearby residential and industrial developments, and other infrastructure.
As a result, the potential additional disturbance impact on these sites of
conservation importance and ecologically sensitive resources during the operation
phase is anticipated to be low.
8.8.4.2 In terms of the planned bat shelter in Pok Wai, given the road section adjacent to
the planned bat shelter would be located in existing developed area/wasteland
habitat in form of viaduct with height of approximately 10 m or above, along with the
retained woodland habitat to the south and east of the planned bat shelter, potential
disturbance impacts such as barrier effect, impact on microclimate and potential
light spill is anticipated to be low. Nevertheless, directional lighting would be
adopted during operation phase to further minimise potential light spill.
8.8.4.3 In addition, apart from the KTMDC, the proposed viaduct section would span a small
area of marsh/reed and pond habitats (e.g. marsh/reed and pond near the
NTMWTW and the planned wetland compensation site under the Ngau Tam Mei
Development). The viaduct section above these habitats would be approximately
13 m wide and 10 m high, ranging from +27 mPD to +31 mPD above ground level.
Given the high clearance, lateral light will penetrate beneath the deck, resulting in
only partial shading of the habitats below. Therefore, the impact from changes in
natural light is considered as low.

and species within or near the Project Boundary during its operation. These habitats
and species are already exposed to regular disturbances under the existing

Obstruction and Disturbance to Flight Corridor
8.8.4.5 The proposed viaduct section across the KTMDC may potentially disrupt the
avifauna flight corridor and disturb ardeids or waterbirds foraging in the KTMDC and
the nearby Sha Po Night Roost. However, since the proposed viaduct section would
be of similar height and close to the existing viaduct of the Yuen Long Highway and
Tsing Long Highway, avifauna species are expected to continue transversing
beneath or above the viaduct sections, similar to current conditions. In terms of
disturbance, the anticipated traffic flow on the proposed viaduct section would also
be comparable to that of the existing viaducts in the KTMDC, where the surrounding
environment is already subjected to constant human disturbance and noise from
heavy traffic. In view of these analogous conditions, the potential obstruction and
disturbance to the flight corridor and foraging ardeids and waterbirds in the KTMDC
and the Sha Po Night Roost are anticipated to be low.
Impact on Water Quality and Water Holding/Water Flow
8.8.4.6 An adequate drainage system would be implemented for the proposed at-grade
road, viaduct, and tunnel, as mentioned in Section 5.6. The potential impact on
water quality due to surface runoff is considered low, and no adverse impacts from
non-point source surface runoff is expected. The drainage system would effectively
prevented surface runoff from entering ecologically sensitive watercourses, as
mentioned in Section 5.6. Consequently, the potential water quality impact on the
surrounding environment, including ponds, semi-natural watercourses, and natural
watercourses, is anticipated to be low, with no adverse effects from non-point
source surface runoff expected.
8.8.4.7 The proposed piles and piers located within the KTMDC would be of similar size
and orientation to the existing bridge piers of the Tsing Long Highway and Yuen
Long Highway. As a result, the impact on the water holding and water flow regime
in the KTMDC could be reduced due to the overall cross-sectional area of the
KTMDC. Furthermore, there would be no additional works or structures that would
affect the water holding capacity of the nearby ponds, semi-natural watercourses,
and natural watercourses during the operation phase of the Project. Therefore, the
potential impact on the water holding and water flow regime of nearby ponds, semi-
natural/natural watercourse, and the KTMDC is considered low.

Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)
Northern Metropolis Highway
– Investigation
Environmental Impact Assessment Report – San Tin Section
Cumulative Ecological Impacts
8.10.1.1 The construction of the Project is tentatively scheduled to commence in 2027, with
a target completion date of 2036 or earlier. A comprehensive list of concurrent
projects is provided in Section 2.9, Table 2.4, and Figure 2.3
8.10.1.2 Potential cumulative impact may arise from the combined effects of concurrent
projects within the Assessment Area, leading to various potential ecological impacts,
including:
• Kwu Tung North New Development Areas (KTN NDA)
• First Phase Development of the New Territories North – San Tin/Lok Ma Chau
Development Node, also known as San Tin Technopole
• Northern Link (NOL) Main Line
• Ngau Tam Mei New Development Area (NTM NDA)
• Ngau Tam Mei Water Treatment Works (NTMWTW) Extension
• The Development of Wetland Conservation Parks (WCP) System, in particular
the Proposed Nam Sang Wai Wetland Conservation Park
• Other sections under Northern Metropolis Highway (NMH)
8.10.1.3 The northern end of the proposed alignment overlaps with the works sites under
the KTN NDA and San Tin Technopole. A large portion of these overlapping areas
mainly comprises developed area/wasteland (including San Tin Highway and
Fanling Highway) and adjacent roadside plantation habitats, with small areas of
hillside wooded habitats such as shrubland and mixed woodland. Considering the
relatively low ecological value of these habitats and the existing disturbances from
adjacent highways, no significant cumulative impact on habitat loss is expected.
8.10.1.4 The proposed alignment overlaps with the work sites associated with the NOL Main
Line, NTM NDA, and the NTM WTW Extension. The overlapping areas with the
NOL Main Line and NTM NDA mainly comprise village/orchard habitat of relatively
low ecological value, while the NTM WTW Extension mainly encompasses
developed area/wasteland habitat. Nonetheless, some wetland habitats (such as
pond and marsh/reed) exist between the proposed NTM NDA and the NTM WTW
Extension, which would be encroached upon by the proposed alignment. While
these wetland habitats may experience some direct impacts, they have been
proposed as a wetland compensation site under the Project. Upon implementing
wetland compensation and enhancement measures, the scattered wetland habitats
with relatively low ecological value in the area are expected to be consolidated and
enhanced as a well-connected, actively managed wetland system, improving
habitat quality and ecological connectivity, thereby creating environmental benefits.
Consequently, no adverse cumulative ecological impacts on the habitats are
expected.
8.10.1.5 The southern portion of the proposed alignment, near Kam Tin River, overlaps with
a wetland compensation site proposed under the NTM NDA (CEDD, 2025), while
the proposed Nam Sang Wai Wetland Conservation Park is situated adjacent to the
proposed alignment, with direct encroachment avoided. The details of the Nam
Sang Wai Wetland Conservation Park are currently under development but are
expected to result in improved and enhanced habitat quality. Information regarding
the compensation wetland under NTM NDA is provided in a separate EIA report.

Additionally , there may be potential disturbances to Sha Po Night Roost and
impacts on species of conservation importance, as discussed in Section 8.8 and

ecological resources. On the other hand, despite a small area of WCA encroaches
within the Project Boundary in Kam Tin, ‘no work zone’ has been designed to avoid

Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)
Northern Metropolis Highway

Environmental Impact Assessment Report – San Tin Section
8.11.2.2 Adoption of Viaduct and Tunnel Sections: The current proposed alignment
incorporates sections of viaduct and tunnel instead of a complete at-grade design,
with ratio of approximately 1: 1.14: 1.95 for at-grade, tunnel, and viaduct sections,
respectively. This design minimises extensive site clearance and site formation
works, significantly reducing the area of habitat loss required under the Project (e.g.
avoiding extensive site formation over low-lying wetland habitats by adopting
viaduct section, and over hillside wooded habitat by adopting tunnel section).
8.11.2.3 Adoption of “No Work Zone”: The Project Boundary includes land required for the
Project, allowing for further refinement by the Contractor’s planning and design
during the construction stage. For impact assessment purposes, all habitats within
the Project Boundary are considered potentially impacted areas to ensure a robust
evaluation of ecological impacts. Nonetheless, considering the large extent of the
Project Boundary and the presence of sensitive ecological resources, a “no work
zone” has been established within the Project Boundary to ensure the habitats and
associated resources are not encroached upon by construction activities, thereby
avoiding direct impacts on these habitats. The “no work zone” delineates areas in
wetland and woodland habitats, including the KTMDC (which encompasses the
modified watercourse habitat within the WCA and the Deep Bay Wetland outside
Ramsar Site Priority Site for Enhanced Conservation), the planned compensation
wetland under the Ngau Tam Mei Development, the woodland habitat east of Pok
Wai, and the pond habitat near NTMWTW.
8.11.2.4 Wetland Habitats at Ngau Tam Mei: Under the original alignment, an interchange
(along with associated site office and ancillary facilities) was proposed to the west
of NTMWTW, resulting in extensive loss of pond and marsh/reed habitats. The
current proposed alignment has been refined, relocating the interchange to the
south of Ngau Tam Mei Tsuen. The direct impact on habitats to the west of
NTMWTW will be limited to the footprint of the pile and pier-related works, as well
as some temporary impacts during the construction phase, thereby avoiding
extensive loss of sensitive wetland habitats.
8.11.2.5 Proposed Nam Sang Wai Wetland Conservation Park: The proposed Nam Sang
Wai Wetland Conservation Park (NSW WCP) is located in close proximity to the
Project Boundary (Figure 8.1 refers). The Project Boundary has been carefully
designed and refined to avoid direct encroachment, preserving these sites of
conservation importance and their associated ecological resources.
8.11.2.6 Watercourses along the Proposed Alignment: A natural watercourse (NTM-S3) has
been identified within the Project Boundary, as discussed in Section 8.8.1.16. The
locations of the proposed pile and pier structures will be fine-tuned, and
construction activities within the Project Boundary will avoid direct encroachment
onto this natural watercourse to prevent adverse ecological impact.

Phasing of Construction Activities to Minimising Habitat Loss

(i.e. KTMDC and ponds near NTMWTW), phasing of construction works would be
adopted in these areas under the Project. This phased construction in KTMDC and
ponds near NTMWTW aims to reduce the scale of disturbance and the total area

multiple phases over a period of at least 2 years. This approach will minimise direct

8.11.3.2 As construction activities would be phased over two years or more, the area
occupied by actual construction (i.e. pond habitat near NTMWTW and KTMDC)
would not exceed half of the designated temporary works area at any given time.
The remaining half would be maintained as pond habitat or watercourse. The
impacted areas from temporary works will be reinstated to their pre-existing
condition as much as practicable before commencing construction on the remaining
half. For instance, steel casing would be used to isolate the surrounding riverbed
when bored pile construction method is employed in KTMDC. The material within
the steel casing will be excavated and confined within the casing for the placement
of reinforcement and concrete for the pile, protecting the watercourse area of
KTMDC outside the steel casing from being affected. Similarly, for pond habitat
near NTMWTW, construction activities would occupy no more than half of the
designated temporary works area at any given time. The temporarily affected ponds
would be reinstated to their pre‑existing conditions before works commence on the
remaining ponds, thereby maintaining at least half of the pond habitat throughout
the construction phase near NTMWTW.
Minimising Construction Phase Impact on Sha Po Night Roost
8.11.3.3 Given the close proximity of the construction works area to the Sha Po Night Roost,
measures will be taken to minimise disturbance to the night roost. Noisy activities,
such as pilling and the use of heavy machinery, should be avoided within 100 m of
the Sha Po ardeid night roost during the period from one hour before sunset to one
hour after sunrise. Sunrise and sunset times will be referenced from the Hong Kong
Observatory. Additionally, other appropriate mitigation measures, such as noise
barriers and good site practices, as detailed in Section 8.11.3.15, will be
implemented near the Sha Po Night Roost to further minimise impacts from
construction activities.
Minimising Construction Phase Impact on Planned Bat Shelter
8.11.3.4 A planned bat shelter is situated in Pok Wai, adjacent to the viaduct section of the
Project. The alignment has been carefully designed to avoid direct impact to this

transplanted to nearby suitable habitat(s) prior to the commencement of site
clearance as a last resort. A detailed pre-construction vegetation survey should be
conducted by a qualified botanist/ecologist with at least seven years of relevant
experience to identify and record the affected individuals. A Plant Protection and
Transplantation Proposal including subsequent monitoring of the affected
individuals, should be prepared by a qualified ecologist/botanist with at least seven
years of relevant experience. The Proposal should be submitted to relevant
government departments (e.g. AFCD and EPD) for approval at least two months
before the commencement of transplantation works.
8.13.1.3 Following transplantation, post-transplantation monitoring should be implemented
to assess the health conditions and survival of the transplanted individuals. A three-
year establishment period should be provided for flora species of conservation
importance. Monitoring should be conducted bi-weekly during the first three months
and monthly throughout the remaining establishment period. Details of post-
transplantation monitoring are provided in the standalone EM&A Manual.
Translocation of Fauna Species of Conservation Importance
8.13.1.4 Fauna species of conservation importance with low mobility should also be
preserved as far as practicable, including one firefly species, namely Motschulsky's
Starworm, and one freshwater fish species, namely Small Snakehead. The species
should be translocated to nearby suitable habitat(s) prior to the commencement of
the relevant parts of the construction works. A detailed pre-construction survey
should be conducted by a suitably qualified ecologist to identify and record affected
individuals prior to the commencement of the relevant construction works. A
Translocation Proposal, including the translocation methodology and subsequent
monitoring of the affected individuals, should be prepared and implemented by a
qualified ecologist with at least seven years of relevant experience. The Proposal
should be submitted to the relevant government departments (e.g. AFCD and EPD)
for approval at least two months before the commencement of translocation works.
Monitoring of Compensatory Woodland
8.13.1.5 Monitoring of the compensatory woodland should be performed on a regular basis
after the first planting to track the survival and establishment of trees, and to
document wildlife use. Surveys at each compensatory woodland location will
commence after the first planting. Randomly selected individuals of each planted
species will be tagged, and their survival rate will be calculated and evaluated.
Supplementary planting will be recommended if necessary. Wildlife use of the
planted vegetation will also be monitored. Details of the monitoring will be included
in the Woodland Compensation Plan to be submitted in the detailed design stage
and agreed with the relevant authorities.
Monitoring of Compensatory Wetland
8.13.1.6 A wetland compensation site will be provided to offset the loss of 2.81 ha of wetland
habitat due to the Project. A Habitat Creation and Management Plan (HCMP)
should be prepared by a qualified ecologist with at least seven years of relevant
experience to form the basis of the proposed wetland compensation site and

Other Minimisation Measures
8.13.1.8 As described in Section 3 and 4, EM&A programmes were recommended to ensure
compliance with the potential air quality and noise impacts (e.g. potential dust
emissions during the construction phase and potential construction noise
exceedances). Monitoring requirements for construction dust emissions and
construction noise are further set out in Section 3 and 4, respectively. Regular site
environmental audits during the construction phase are also recommended to
ensure proper implementation of mitigation measures and good site practices.
Details of the EM&A programme are provided in a standalone EM&A Manual.
8.13.1.9 As described in Section 5, water quality monitoring and regular site inspections
would be undertaken during the construction to ensure that the recommended
mitigation measures for water quality are properly implemented. Details on water
quality monitoring requirements are further set out in the Water Quality Impact
Assessment (Section 5) and the standalone EM&A Manual.
Conclusion
8.14.1.1 The ecological impact assessment for the Project has been conducted in
accordance with the EIA Study Brief No. ESB-373/2025, the criteria and guidelines
of the EIAO-TM Annexes 8 and 16, as well as relevant EIAO Guidance Notes.
8.14.1.2 The Assessment Area includes areas within a 500 m distance from the San Tin
section of the NMH alignment and associated works (i.e. the Project Boundary).
Several recognised sites of conservation importance, including Priority Sites for
Enhanced Conservation, Lam Tsuen Country Park (LTCP), Conservation Area (CA),
Wetland Conservation Area (WCA), Wetland Buffer Area (WBA), and other
ecologically sensitive resources such as the proposed Nam Sang Wai Wetland
Conservation Park (NSW WCP), were identified within the Assessment Area. The
Project Boundary encroaches into small areas of WCA, WBA, and Deep Bay
Wetland outside Ramsar Site Priority Sites for Enhanced Conservation, but the
encroached habitats are limited to man-made habitats, including developed
area/wasteland, roadside plantation, and small section of modified watercourse, all
of which are subject to regular disturbance (e.g. traffic and human activities along
the existing highway). For CA, impacts may arise from the loss of woodland
habitats, which will be compensated with a Woodland Compensation Plan.

Agreement No. CE 4/2024 (HY)
Northern Metropolis Highway
– Investigation
Environmental Impact Assessment Report – San Tin Section
8.14.1.3 A total of 15 habitat types were identified during the ecological survey within the
500 m Assessment Area, including woodland, mixed woodland, shrubland,
grassland, plantation, village/orchard, developed area/wasteland, agricultural land,
seasonally wet grassland, marsh/reed, pond, natural watercourse, semi-natural
watercourse, modified watercourse, and mitigation wetland. These habitats are
generally considered to have “low” or “low to moderate” ecological values, except
for woodland, ponds within WCA and WBA, YLBFEW, and Kam Tin Main Drainage
Channel (i.e. YL-S1), which are considered as “moderate” ecological value, as well
as Sha Po Marsh (outside of Project Boundary), which is considered to have
“moderate to high” value.
8.14.1.4 8.14.1.5 Direct impacts arising from the Project include direct loss of habitats and vegetation
due to the proposed alignment and temporary works. Avoidance and minimisation
measures (e.g. refinement of alignment and establishment of “no work zone” during
construction activities) have been considered to reduce and minimise the direct and
indirect impacts to these habitats. Woodland and wetland compensation measures
have also been recommended to mitigate the inevitable loss of ecologically
sensitive habitats. Direct impact may also potentially arise from the potential direct
injury or mortality of species of conservation importance within the Project Boundary,
particularly species with low mobility, including the flora species Cycad-fern, Hong
Kong Pavetta and Incense Tree, as well as the firefly species Motschulsky's
Starworm and the freshwater fish species Small Snakehead. Pre-construction site
checks with associated transplantation and translocation exercises are
recommended.
On the other hand, indirect impacts such as disturbance impact to adjacent
recognised sites of conservation importance and ecologically sensitive resources
(such as Sha Po Night Roost and a planned bat shelter), as well as night-time
disturbance and potential impacts on water quality, water holding, and water flow in
the ponds and watercourses, may be induced by the construction and operation of
the Project. Measures such as providing screening, using directional lighting,
following good site practice, and implementing other noise, air, and water quality
mitigation measures are recommended. Moreover, specific measures for the Sha
Po Night Roost are also recommended, including a 100 m Buffer Area for the night
roost, where noisy works would be subject to timing control. The use of non-
transparent or non-glaring materials is also recommended to avoid and minimise
potential direct impacts to the habitats and associated wildlife within and adjacent
to the Project Site.
8.14.1.6 With the implementation of the aforementioned mitigation measures, no adverse
ecological impacts are anticipated to arise from the Project.
